question: In 2015, the time spent by Commission staff in replying to parliamentary questions was the equivalent of at least 76 full-time equivalents. Commissioner Timmermans indicated that this worked out at approximately EUR 490 per question.1 1.
How many full-time staff equivalents are engaged in handling parliamentary questions today?
What is the approximate average cost per parliamentary question?

Can the Commission elaborate on Commissioner Timmermans explanation that ‘each written reply to a parliamentary question goes through a process of attribution, drafting, validation, interservice coordination, collegiate endorsement, and finally translation’?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.7.2024) 1.and 2. Using the same methodology as in 2015, the Commission estimates that, for 2023, at least 16 full-time equivalents (FTE) were used to prepare replies to the 3 607 written parliamentary questions received, at an approximate cost of EUR 627 per question. 3.

In accordance with Article 230 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union and in order to respect the principle of collegiality, parliamentary questions are answered by the Commission and not by individual Commissioners. Replies are subject to a rigorous internal decision-making process which considers all the policy perspectives at stake. This process consists of several stages.

First, the Commission’s Secretariat-General evaluates and assigns the question to the lead service and Commissioner. As the questions are often complex and contain sub-questions, several associated services are involved in the preparation of the draft reply. Second, in accordance with the Commission’s working methods, the lead service prepares the draft reply.

Third, an inter-service consultation is launched allowing services concerned to contribute to the draft reply from their own policy perspective. Fourth, the draft reply is validated by the cabinets of the lead and associated Commissioners.

Fifth, the draft reply gets political validation by the College of Commissioners via a written adoption procedure and is translated into the language of the author, Member of the European Parliament. As a final step, the Commission Secretariat-General transmits the reply to the services of the European Parliament.

This thorough process ensures that the reply provided to the Member of the European Parliament is reflective of the Commission as a whole and is of the highest possible quality and political relevance.

It becomes clear from this collegial process that the Commission does not have dedicated staff, who are engaged only to respond to written parliamentary questions, but that the work is spread across services depending on the subject matter and complexity of a parliamentary question.
